hints: Define a state using prefixes of the two strings: what is the minimum cost to convert the first i characters of word1 into the first j characters of word2?
When the current characters match, no new operation is needed. When they differ, consider insertion, deletion, and replacement.

Only the previous DP row is needed for the next row, so the memory can be reduced to one dimension.
title: Edit Distance Problem

notes: Each insertion, deletion, or replacement has cost 1.
An empty string is valid because the minimum length of either word is zero.
A one-dimensional dynamic-programming array is sufficient because only the previous row is required.
constraints: word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: horse -> rorse (replace 'h' with 'r'), rorse -> rose (remove 'r'), rose -> ros (remove 'e').
A minimum sequence of insert, delete, and replacement operations converts intention into execution in 5 operations.

content.problemStatement:
You receive two strings `word1` and `word2`, output *the smallest number of operations required to convert `word1` to `word2`*.

You have the following three operations permitted on a word:

* Insert a character
* Delete a character
* Replace a character

notes: All inputs use the JSON argument format [word1,word2].
All hidden strings satisfy the lowercase-English-letter constraint and length limit.
The judge compares the returned integer exactly.
The recurrence is dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] when characters match, otherwise 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]).
Swapping the strings so the shorter one is used for the DP columns minimizes auxiliary memory.
Empty-prefix states are initialized to their prefix lengths.
solution.approach: Use dynamic programming. Let dp[j] be the minimum edit distance between the processed prefix of word1 and the first j characters of word2. If the current characters match, carry the diagonal value; otherwise take one plus the minimum of insertion, deletion, and replacement. Keep only the previous and current rows, using O(min(m,n)) auxiliary space.

better.complexity: O(m * n) time and O(m * n) memory.
better.description: Memoize the recursive state (i,j), where each state represents the minimum cost to convert the first i characters of word1 to the first j characters of word2.

optimal.complexity: O(m * n) time and O(min(m,n)) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: Use iterative dynamic programming while retaining only the previous row. Each state considers insertion, deletion, and replacement, and matching characters use the diagonal state without adding cost.

bruteForce.complexity: Exponential time in the worst case and O(m+n) recursion depth.
bruteForce.description: Recursively try insertion, deletion, and replacement at every mismatch. This explores a large overlapping state space and becomes exponential without memoization.

followUps: Can you reduce the auxiliary space from O(m*n) to O(min(m,n))?
How would the recurrence change if substitutions had a cost different from insertions and deletions?
What changes would be needed to recover an actual minimum sequence of edit operations rather than only its cost?

hidden.label: Insert all characters into empty word
Delete all characters to reach empty word
Edit requiring insertion before matching suffix
Replacement path with shifted middle character
Common suffix after two leading edits

learningObjectives: Model string transformation problems with dynamic programming.
Derive the edit-distance recurrence from the three allowed operations.
Optimize a two-dimensional DP solution to one-dimensional auxiliary space.
